newsitem.title: USA: American civil rights leader to be buried in Harlem.
newsitem.headline: American civil rights leader to be buried in Harlem.

text.p: Civil rights activist and PanAfricanist Audley "Queen Mother" Moore will be buried on Friday, a spokesman for the Ethiopian Orthodox Coptic Church in Harlem said on Thursday.

An elder stateswoman among African-Americans and one of the few women to appear on the platform at Louis Farrakhan's Million Man March last October, Moore died last week in a Brooklyn nursing home at the age of 98.
Her remains were to be escorted along the streets of Harlem from the Coptic Church to the larger Mount Olivet Baptist church for a Coptic funeral ceremony, he said.
A tireless political organiser and charismatic speaker, she travelled extensively in the United States and Africa.

Moore's friends ranged from Marcus Garvey, a Jamaican immigrant who started a back-to-Africa movement in the 1920s, to South African President Nelson Mandela, whose release from jail she attended in South Africa, and former New York City Mayor David Dinkins.
She was given the Akan title of queen mother or "ohemaa" -- ruler of the women and mother of princes -- by the Asantes during one of her first trips to Ghana.

As part of her uncompromising push for black empowerment, she was active in the then-separatist Republic of New Africa and took her fight for reparations from the United States government for centuries of work by enslaved Africans as far as the Organisation of African Unity in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

"They stole our language, they stole our culture. They stole us from our mothers and fathers and took our names away from us. They worked us free of charge 18 hours a day, seven days a week, under the lash, for centuries. We lost over 100 million lives in the traffic of slavery," Moore once said.
She also pressed for a memorial to the captives who were forced into slave ships at Goree Island, Senegal.
Moore was born in July 1898 in New Iberia, Louisiana. Her family history included a grandfather who was lynched and a slave grandmother who was raped by a white man.
Her parents died when she was 9 and she had to drop out of school and go to work, eventually training as a hairdresser.

She became politicized at 19 or 20 after hearing Marcus Garvey speak in New Orleans. A firm believer in working through active groups, she went on to become prominent in the Communist Party from 1933 to 1950, before becaming a Republican and then a Democrat.
She fought for integration of the military and Major League Baseball. She helped organise pressure for prisoner rights and worked to expand black political representation.
Moore's husband Frank Warner died in 1967. She is survived by a son, Thomas O. Warner of Philadelphia and five grandchildren.
